newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia has no reason to apologise on race - PM.
newsitem.headline: Australia has no reason to apologise on race - PM.

text.p: Prime Minister John Howard, trying to put a damaging race row behind him, said on Friday Australians had nothing to apologise for on the issue of race.

At a news conference marking the end of the parliamentary year, Howard said a charge by a leading Aborigine on Thursday that his conservative government had encouraged a rise in racial intolerance was "over the top".
"I don't believe Australia is a racist country," Howard said. "There are racists in Australia, of course there are, there are racists in every country."
But he added: "It is very important that we don't sound apologetic to the rest of the world on the issue of racism because our credentials are very creditable indeed".

"We are far ahead of most and these are certainly not things we should be defensive or apologetic about whilst acknowledging, as I frequently have, there are dark stains on our history of which the treatment of the Aborigines is obviously the most prominent."
Aborigines were masscared, poisoned and used as slave labour by Australia's early white settlers. There are now some 300,000 Aborigines in Australia's 18 million multi-cultural population.

Howard's conservative coalition and other mainstream parties have struggled to contain a race row spurred by independent politician Pauline Hanson, a fish and chip shop owner from conservative Queensland state.
Hanson used her maiden parliamentary speech to warn that Asians, who make up five percent of the Australian population, could swamp the country and called for an immediate moratorium on immigration.

Tapping into public resentment at the policies of the Labor government ousted by Howard in March, Hanson also complained that Aborigines and other indigenous groups received unfair economic assistance from government.

The fall-out from her remarks has been widely reported in Asia, to the dismay of Australian businesses trying to exploit the Asian marketplace, and Howard has been condemned for failing to end the damaging row.
Although Howard consistently denounced racism and said his government had no intention of turning its back on non-discriminatory immigration, he refused to openly condemn Hanson for her remarks.

On Thursday, more criticism came from official aboriginal human rights watchdog, Mick Dodson, who said Howard's "total lack of leadership" had given people with extreme views a licence to be intolerant.

"I feel Mr Dodson's remarks were inaccurate and quite intemperate. They didn't really do his own cause a great deal of justice," Howard replied on Friday, announcing plans to tour aboriginal communities next year to better understand the plight of Australia's most disadvantaged group.
